claim: Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be the most challenging, constantly present infectious disease worldwide, with 7.5 million newly reported cases and 1.3 million deaths per year.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be the most challenging, constantly present infectious disease worldwide, with 7.5 million newly reported cases and 1.3 million deaths per year (World Health Organization, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2021

claim: The resurgence of TB is due to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
source: The resurgence of TB due to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic (World Health Organization, 2023) underscores the interconnected nature of global health and economic issues with TB incidence and control.
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2023

claim: The causative agents of TB are members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis) complex.
source: The causative agents of TB are members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis) complex.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about TB etiology

claim: M. tuberculosis bacteria can incur a sustained threat to humanity thanks to their long-term latency and their highly unresponsive nature to antibiotics.
source: These obligate pathogen bacteria can incur a sustained threat to humanity thanks to their long-term latency (Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009) and their highly unresponsive nature to antibiotics (Hett and Rubin, 2008; Jankute et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009; Hett and Rubin, 2008; Jankute et al., 2015

claim: Drug tolerance arises when certain bacterial populations are temporarily able to survive antibiotic pressure in the absence of drug resistance-conferring mutations.
source: Drug tolerance arises when certain bacterial populations are temporarily able to survive antibiotic pressure in the absence of drug resistance-conferring mutations.
evidence: Definition provided in the manuscript

claim: Upon exposure to bactericidal drugs, tolerant mycobacteria are eliminated at a lower rate than the fully susceptible population.
source: Upon exposure to bactericidal drugs, tolerant mycobacteria are eliminated at a lower rate than the fully susceptible population (Balaban et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Balaban et al., 2019

claim: Several interconnected biological pathways are involved in the emergence and establishment of a drug-tolerant state including metabolic slowdown, metabolic shifting, cell wall thickening, and transcriptional regulation-guided adaptation.
source: Several interconnected biological pathways are involved in the emergence and establishment of a drug-tolerant state (Boshoff et al., 2004; Walter et al., 2015) including metabolic slowdown, metabolic shifting, cell wall thickening, and transcriptional regulation-guided adaptation (Goossens et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boshoff et al., 2004; Walter et al., 2015; Goossens et al., 2020

claim: Several efflux pumps are upregulated under antibiotic stress.
source: For example, several efflux pumps are upregulated under antibiotic stress (Louw et al., 2011; Wiuff et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Louw et al., 2011; Wiuff et al., 2005

claim: Horizontal gene transfer does not appear to function in members of the M. tuberculosis complex.
source: Interestingly, horizontal gene transfer, which is a major contributor to antibiotic resistance in other species does not appear to function in members of the M. tuberculosis complex (Gray and Derbyshire, 2018; Madacki et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray and Derbyshire, 2018; Madacki et al., 2021

claim: Any resistant genotype in M. tuberculosis can only emerge by de novo mutagenesis.
source: Therefore, any resistant genotype can only emerge by de novo mutagenesis.
evidence: Logical inference from the absence of horizontal gene transfer

claim: The M. tuberculosis population within individual TB patients can be more heterogeneous than was traditionally thought.
source: It is now commonly accepted that the M. tuberculosis population within individual TB patients can be more heterogeneous than was traditionally thought (Hingley-Wilson et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hingley-Wilson et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015

claim: The coexistence of both drug-resistant and drug-sensitive strains in a single patient has been described in clinical isolates.
source: The coexistence of both drug-resistant and drug-sensitive strains in a single patient, or even several drug-resistant strains with discrete drug resistance-conferring mutations has been described in clinical isolates (Asare-Baah et al., 2021; Lozano et al., 2021; Pérez-Lago et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asare-Baah et al., 2021; Lozano et al., 2021; Pérez-Lago et al., 2016

claim: The occurrence of mixed infections reached 19% of the examined patients in South Africa.
source: Warren et al. found that the occurrence of mixed infections reached 19% of the examined patients in South Africa by using a PCR-based strain classification method (Warren et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warren et al., 2004

claim: Mixed infections can result from simultaneously or sequentially acquired infections by different strains or genomic evolution of a strain under mutagenic pressure within the host.
source: Mixed infections can result from (i) simultaneously or sequentially acquired infections by different strains or (ii) genomic evolution of a strain under mutagenic pressure within the host (termed microevolution) and consequent coexistence of several populations.
evidence: Logical inference about possible mechanisms

claim: The lineage 2 strains of the Beijing genotype exhibited a higher mutation rate.
source: For example, the lineage 2 strains of the Beijing genotype exhibited a higher mutation rate (Ford et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ford et al., 2011

claim: Some studies found stable M. tuberculosis genomes with no or only a few emerging genomic changes over prolonged periods of treatment.
source: On the other hand, others found stable M. tuberculosis genomes with no or only a few emerging genomic changes over prolonged periods of treatment (Herranz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herranz et al., 2018

claim: M. smegmatis shares most DNA metabolic pathways with the medically relevant Mycobacterium species.
source: This non-pathogenic relative of the medically relevant Mycobacterium species shares most DNA metabolic pathways with the medically relevant strains.
evidence: General statement about M. smegmatis as a model organism

claim: There is a high degree of conservation between the DNA repair enzymes in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis.
source: Davis and Forse compared the sequences of proteins involved in base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair pathways in E. coli and their homologs in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis and found that there is a high degree of conservation between the DNA repair enzymes in M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis (Davis and Forse, 2009; Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis and Forse, 2009; Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2012

claim: The basic strategy used to repair DNA lesions is conserved across mycobacterial species.
source: Bioinformatic analyses of completely sequenced mycobacterial genomes, including M. tuberculosis (Camus et al., 2002), M. leprae (Silva et al., 2022), M. bovis (Garnier et al., 2003; Zimpel et al., 2017), M. avium, M. paratuberculosis, and M. smegmatis (Mohan et al., 2015) also demonstrated through the comparison of genes participating in many of the DNA repair/recombination pathways that the basic strategy used to repair DNA lesions is conserved (Singh, 2017; Singh et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on mycobacterial genomes

claim: The M. tuberculosis, M. smegmatis, and M. leprae LexA proteins are functionally conserved at the level of DNA binding.
source: Durbach et.al, investigated mycobacterial SOS response and showed that the M. tuberculosis, M. smegmatis, and M. leprae LexA proteins are functionally conserved at the level of DNA binding (Durbach et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Durbach et al., 1997

claim: The enzymes of thymidylate biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis show high conservation.
source: In our earlier paper, we also compared the enzymes of thymidylate biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis and found high conservation (Pecsi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pecsi et al., 2012

claim: The bacteriostatic drugs INH and EMB caused moderate CFU decrease in liquid cultures compared to the control.
source: The bacteriostatic drugs INH and EMB caused moderate CFU decrease in liquid cultures compared to the control (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with their mechanism of action (Alland et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Alland et al., 2000

claim: Following RIF, CIP, and MMC treatments, cells elongated by more than twofold.
source: Specifically, following RIF, CIP, and MMC treatments, we observed cells elongating by more than twofold, whereas INH and EMB treatments led to a reduction in cell length.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1

claim: INH and EMB treatments led to a reduction in cell length.
source: Specifically, following RIF, CIP, and MMC treatments, we observed cells elongating by more than twofold, whereas INH and EMB treatments led to a reduction in cell length.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 1

claim: The combination treatment did not affect the cell size.
source: The combination treatment did not affect the cell size (Figure 1 and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and Table 1

claim: M. smegmatis exhibits an intrinsic resistance to PZA.
source: However, M. smegmatis was reported to exhibit an intrinsic resistance to PZA (Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 1999

claim: PZA treatment alone, even at high concentrations in acidic conditions, did not affect cell viability in our experiments.
source: Indeed, PZA treatment alone, even at high concentrations in acidic conditions, did not affect cell viability in our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Bacteria produced on average 230 generations during the 60 day treatment.
source: We measured an average generation time of 6.3±0.35 hr on the plate within the timeframe of a single passage. Therefore, bacteria produced on average 230 generations during the 60 day treatment.
evidence: Calculated from measured generation time

claim: The M. smegmatis ancestor strain carried 151 various mutations compared to the M. smegmatis reference genome deposited in the GenBank.
source: According to the WGS results, our M. smegmatis ancestor strain carried 151 various mutations compared to the M. smegmatis reference genome deposited in the GenBank.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: A maximum of one mutation per lineage occurred during the 60 day drug treatments.
source: We found that a maximum of one mutation per lineage occurred during the 60 day drug treatments.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data analysis

claim: A maximum of one mutation per lineage was detected during the 60- or 120 day mock treatment.
source: Also, a maximum of one mutation per lineage was detected during the 60- or 120 day mock treatment (16 newly generated mutations for 56 lineages).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data analysis

claim: The mutation rate of untreated M. smegmatis mc2155 strain is 1×10–10.
source: We calculated a 1×10–10 mutation rate for our untreated M. smegmatis mc2155 strain.
evidence: Calculated from whole genome sequencing data

claim: The mutation rates of all treated lineages fell in one order of magnitude (4×10–11 - 3×10–10) except for the UV treatment.
source: To our great surprise, the mutation rates of all treated lineages fell in one order of magnitude (4×10–11 - 3×10–10) except for the UV treatment used for positive control (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2B

claim: No sign of adaptive changes was found in the mutations analyzed except those obtained following the UV treatment.
source: We analyzed each mutation except those obtained following the UV treatment and found no sign of adaptive changes (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis shown in Table 2

claim: The MIC values for the MA strains were higher than those of the mock-treated strains, indicating phenotypic adaptation to the applied drugs.
source: Contrary to the mutation rate results obtained from genomic sequencing data, the MIC values for the MA strains were higher than those of the mock-treated strains (comparable data in line with Nyinoh, 2019), indicating phenotypic adaptation to the applied drugs (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by MIC measurement data shown in Figure 2C

claim: For the EMB treatment, no increase in MIC was observed.
source: However, for the EMB treatment, we observed no increase in MIC, despite repeating the experiment several times.
evidence: Supported by repeated experimental observations

claim: Treatments with INH and EMB show similar patterns in the expression levels with an overall downregulation of DNA repair genes.
source: Treatments with the two antibiotics affecting cell wall synthesis (INH and EMB) show similar patterns in the expression levels with an overall downregulation of DNA repair genes.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: CIP and MMC induce a pattern marked by a moderate to strong overexpression of nucleotide excision and double-strand break (DSB) repair genes, respectively.
source: On the contrary, CIP and MMC, drugs directly targeting DNA integrity induce a pattern marked by a moderate to strong overexpression of nucleotide excision and double-strand break (DSB) repair genes, respectively (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: DNA polymerases DinB2 and DnaE2 involved in DNA repair pathways are strongly overexpressed following CIP and MMC treatments.
source: DNA polymerases DinB2 and DnaE2 involved in these DNA repair pathways are also strongly overexpressed (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: RIF does not seem to induce any change in the expression pattern of the investigated genes except for the Ahp peroxiredoxin.
source: RIF, the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor does not seem to induce any change in the expression pattern of the investigated genes except for the Ahp peroxiredoxin (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: As a result of the first line combination (COMBO) treatment, 14 out of 38 investigated genes are significantly (p<0.05) upregulated.
source: As a result of the first line combination (COMBO) treatment, 14 out of 38 investigated genes are significantly (p<0.05) upregulated.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: More than fourfold upregulation can be measured for 5 members of the base excision repair pathway following COMBO treatment.
source: More than fourfold upregulation can be measured for 5 members of the base excision repair pathway.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: The MutT2 dNTP pool sanitization enzyme and the error-prone DNA polymerases are strongly upregulated following COMBO treatment.
source: In addition, the MutT2 dNTP pool sanitization enzyme and the error-prone DNA polymerases are also strongly upregulated. (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: The DSB repair enzymes are exempt from the overall upregulation tendency following COMBO treatment.
source: Interestingly, however, the DSB repair enzymes are exempt from this overall upregulation tendency (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: The strongest measured effect of all treatments is the 17-fold expression increase of the KatG1 peroxidase following COMBO treatment.
source: The strongest measured effect of all is the 17-fold expression increase of the KatG1 peroxidase (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: The CIP treatment resulted in approximately sevenfold increases in dATP and dTTP concentrations accompanied by a decrease in the dGTP concentration.
source: The CIP treatment resulted in the most remarkable differences in particular for dATP and dTTP concentrations which increased ~ sevenfold accompanied by a decrease in the dGTP concentration (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: RIF and MMC treatments promoted an increase in the dGTP and dCTP pools.
source: RIF and MMC treatments promoted an increase in the dGTP and dCTP pools (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: The INH treatment coincided with a decreased concentration of purine nucleotides.
source: The INH treatment coincided with a decreased concentration of purine nucleotides (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: In EMB-treated cells, very low levels of all dNTPs were measured.
source: while in EMB-treated cells we could measure very low levels of all dNTPs (Figure 4C and H).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: In the combination treatment, no significant differences in dNTP levels were measured.
source: In the combination treatment, we could not measure significant differences (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: The dGTP pool decreased in both absolute and relative terms across all treatments where dNTP pool changes were observed.
source: The dGTP pool decreased in both absolute and relative terms across all treatments where dNTP pool changes were observed (Figure 4B–F and G, respectively).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: A smaller cell size coincides with a lower cellular dNTP concentration.
source: A smaller cell size coincides with a lower cellular dNTP concentration, while no clear correlation is observed between drug-induced cell length increase and dNTP pool expansion (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4I

claim: No clear correlation is observed between drug-induced cell length increase and dNTP pool expansion.
source: A smaller cell size coincides with a lower cellular dNTP concentration, while no clear correlation is observed between drug-induced cell length increase and dNTP pool expansion (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4I

claim: The estimated rate of emergence of the tolerance for CIP is three orders of magnitude higher than the mutation rate calculated based on WGS (10–7 vs. 10–10).
source: We found that the estimated rate of emergence of the tolerance for CIP is three orders of magnitude higher than the mutation rate calculated based on WGS (10–7 vs. 10–10, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of fluctuation assay and WGS data

claim: Following a 24–96 hr exposure to a sublethal 0.3 μg/ml dose of CIP, a phenotypic tolerance appears in a significant portion of the cells to an otherwise lethal 0.5 μg/ml dose.
source: Furthermore, following a 24–96 hr exposure to a sublethal 0.3 μg/ml dose of CIP, a phenotypic tolerance appears in a significant portion of the cells to an otherwise lethal 0.5 μg/ml dose (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The tolerant cell population increased with the length of the preincubation time before reaching a maximum.
source: The tolerant cell population increased with the length of the preincubation time before reaching a maximum (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: After 96 hr pretreatment with CIP, a single mutation in a gene encoding an uncharacterized protein probably involved in lipid metabolism (MSMEG_6151) was detected in all measured samples.
source: After pretreatment, DNA was isolated from colonies on five parallel plates for each of the three biological replicates, followed by WGS (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). In all measured samples, we detected a single mutation in a gene encoding an uncharacterized protein probably involved in lipid metabolism (MSMEG_6151; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 2

claim: No mutations were detected in the genomes of colonies grown at the higher CIP concentration (0.5 µg/ml).
source: We also sequenced the genomes of colonies grown at the higher CIP concentration (0.5 µg/ml) and detected no mutations.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: Measured and estimated mycobacterial mutation rates in the earlier literature are in the order of 10–10 /bp/generation.
source: Measured and estimated mycobacterial mutation rates in the earlier literature are in the order of 10–10 /bp/generation (Ragheb et al., 2013, Kucukyildirim et al., 2016, Ford et al., 2011, Colangeli et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: This low constitutive mutation rate by itself does not explain the biological diversity observed in clinical isolates.
source: This low constitutive mutation rate by itself does not explain the biological diversity observed in clinical isolates (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012

claim: Even without pretreatment, a tolerance rate on the order of 10–7/generation was observed for CIP, consistent with literature data from fluctuation assays.
source: Even without pretreatment, a tolerance rate on the order of 10–7/generation was observed for CIP, consistent with literature data from fluctuation assays (Bergval et al., 2012; David, 1970).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Bergval et al., 2012; David, 1970

claim: In the mutation accumulation assay, the number of mutations did not change significantly compared to the untreated control.
source: However, in the mutation accumulation assay, the number of mutations did not change significantly compared to the untreated control.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data analysis

claim: The mutation rate increase was only significant in the case of the UV treatment serving as a positive control for the experiments.
source: The mutation rate increase was only significant in the case of the UV treatment serving as a positive control for the experiments (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The emergence of drug resistance in this study is solely attributed to phenotypic factors.
source: Our findings imply that the emergence of drug resistance in this study is solely attributed to phenotypic factors.
evidence: Inference from the experimental results showing no genetic changes but phenotypic tolerance

claim: The downregulation of KatG1 and Nei2 in response to INH treatment is in line with redox potential change and might indicate a reduced cellular redox potential.
source: Redox potential change is a well-known and common phenotypic response to INH in mycobacteria (Niki et al., 2012). The downregulation of KatG1 and Nei2 in response to our INH treatment (Figure 3) is in line with this and might indicate a reduced cellular redox potential.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data and citation to Niki et al., 2012

claim: KatG1 is the enzyme that activates the prodrug INH.
source: KatG1 is the enzyme that activates the prodrug INH (Niki et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Niki et al., 2012

claim: The downregulation of KatG1 decreases the active drug concentration and increases the tolerance of M. smegmatis against INH.
source: therefore, the downregulation of this enzyme decreases the active drug concentration and increases the tolerance of M. smegmatis against INH.
evidence: Logical inference from the role of KatG1 in INH activation

claim: In the case of the first-line combination treatment, KatG1 was highly upregulated, indicating high ROS levels in the cell.
source: In the case of the first-line combination treatment, however, KatG1 was highly upregulated, indicating high ROS levels in the cell (Wayne and Diaz, 1986).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data and citation to Wayne and Diaz, 1986

claim: High ROS levels are known to cause damage to nucleobases and the nucleotide pool is a major effector of oxidative stress-induced genotoxic damage.
source: High ROS levels are known to cause damage to nucleobases and the nucleotide pool is a major effector of oxidative stress-induced genotoxic damage (Rai, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rai, 2010

claim: Upregulation in dNTP pool sanitation, base- and nucleotide-repair pathways was observed following COMBO treatment.
source: In line with this, we observed upregulation in dNTP pool sanitation, base- and nucleotide-repair pathways which play crucial roles in preventing and repairing DNA damage caused by oxidative stress.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3

claim: The observed synergistic effect clearly results from the combination of first-line drugs, as this effect was not observed when applying the drugs individually.
source: The observed synergistic effect clearly results from the combination of first-line drugs, as we did not observe this effect when applying the drugs individually.
evidence: Inference from comparison of combination vs. individual drug treatments

claim: The observed upregulation of the relevant DNA repair enzymes might account for the low mutation rate even under drug pressure.
source: The observed upregulation of the relevant DNA repair enzymes might account for the low mutation rate even under drug pressure.
evidence: Inference from the correlation between DNA repair upregulation and low mutation rates

claim: Error-prone polymerases DinB2 and DnaE2 exhibited significant upregulation without inducing a mutator phenotype.
source: Notably, error-prone polymerases DinB2 and DnaE2 exhibited significant upregulation without inducing a mutator phenotype.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and WGS data

claim: Error-prone and error-free repair mechanisms are coactivated, predominantly resulting in error-free repairs.
source: This indicates that error-prone and error-free repair mechanisms are coactivated, predominantly resulting in error-free repairs.
evidence: Inference from the observation of upregulated error-prone polymerases without increased mutation rates

claim: Increased or imbalanced dNTP pools induce mutagenesis in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: It has been shown that increased or imbalanced dNTP pools induce mutagenesis in prokaryotes Gon et al., 2011 and eukaryotes (Pai and Kearsey, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gon et al., 2011 and Pai and Kearsey, 2017

claim: When treating the cells with frontline drugs EMB and INH individually, the observed reductions in dNTP pool sizes and cell size aligned well with the concurrent downregulated transcript levels.
source: When treating the cells with frontline drugs EMB and INH individually, the observed reductions in dNTP pool sizes and cell size (as illustrated in Figure 4H–I) aligned well with the concurrent downregulated transcript levels (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by correlation of dNTP, cell size, and gene expression data

claim: Resting states of bacteria have been characterized by a decrease in cell size and dATP levels.
source: Resting states of bacteria have also been characterized by a decrease in cell size and dATP levels (Rittershaus et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rittershaus et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016

claim: The combined treatment yielded the least significant alteration from the untreated control compared to all monotreatments.
source: The combined treatment yielded the least significant alteration from the untreated control compared to all monotreatments (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: An elevation in the dNTP pools during CIP treatment aligns with the substantial increase in the expression of DNA repair synthesis genes.
source: This observation, particularly in the case of CIP treatment, aligns with the substantial increase in the expression of DNA repair synthesis genes, as depicted in Figure 3.
evidence: Supported by correlation of dNTP and gene expression data

claim: Only the CIP treatment led to a notable dNTP imbalance and a substantial overall rise in dNTP pools, due to elevated levels of dTTP and dATP.
source: Among all administered treatments, only the CIP treatment led to a notable dNTP imbalance and a substantial overall rise in dNTP pools, due to elevated levels of dTTP and dATP.
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: The dGTP level decreased with all drug treatments.
source: Interestingly, the dGTP level decreased with all drug treatments.
evidence: Supported by dNTP measurement data shown in Figure 4

claim: dGTP may play a role in a general stress response.
source: This finding suggests that dGTP may play a role in a general stress response.
evidence: Speculation based on the consistent decrease of dGTP across treatments

claim: An excess of dGTP has been identified as a significant contributor to mutations.
source: Specifically, an excess of dGTP has been identified as a significant contributor to mutations (Martomo and Mathews, 2002; Schmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martomo and Mathews, 2002; Schmidt et al., 2019

claim: In mycobacteria, dGTP is the most abundant dNTP species.
source: However, in mycobacteria, a unique scenario exists where dGTP is the most abundant dNTP species (Pancsa et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Pancsa et al., 2022

claim: Mycobacterial genomes are characterized by a high GC content.
source: and mycobacterial genomes are characterized by a high GC content (Andersson and Sharp, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andersson and Sharp, 1996

claim: A reduction in dGTP levels may contribute to minimizing DNA lesions by enhancing proofreading efficiency.
source: A reduction in dGTP levels in this context may contribute to minimizing DNA lesions by enhancing proofreading efficiency.
evidence: Speculation based on the role of dGTP in mutagenesis

claim: The hypothesis that systematic antibiotics treatment induces mutation rate increase in M. smegmatis failed.
source: Our hypothesis that systematic antibiotics treatment induces mutation rate increase in M. smegmatis failed, as we did not observe any significant impact of antibiotics on mutability in laboratory conditions.
evidence: Conclusion from the experimental results

claim: Only in the case of CIP treatment could a slightly (but not significantly) elevated mutation rate be detected.
source: Only in the case of CIP treatment, a second-line TB drug known for directly inducing DNA damage, could we detect a slightly (but not significantly) elevated mutation rate.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: The treatment of M. smegmatis with the clinically used combination therapy drugs did not induce a mutator effect.
source: The treatment of M. smegmatis with the clinically used combination therapy drugs did not induce a mutator effect, quite the opposite.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data

claim: The observed activation of DNA repair processes likely mitigates mutation pressure, ensuring genome stability.
source: The observed activation of DNA repair processes likely mitigates mutation pressure, ensuring genome stability.
evidence: Inference from the correlation between DNA repair activation and low mutation rates

claim: In at least 17% of TB treatments, resistance to RIF or RIF+INH (called multidrug resistance) emerges.
source: In at least 17% of the treatments, resistance to RIF or RIF+INH (called multidrug resistance) emerges (World Health Organization, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2023

claim: There are two models for the development of drug-resistant TB: acquired and transmitted drug resistance.
source: There are two models for the development of drug-resistant TB: acquired and transmitted drug resistance.

source: The acquired drug resistance model suggests that resistance is developed within patients with active TB through microevolution (Ley et al., 2019).

claim: Distinguishing between acquired and transmitted resistance is not straightforward based solely on allele variants found in the sputum.
source: However, it is crucial to note that distinguishing between acquired and transmitted resistance is not straightforward based solely on allele variants found in the sputum.

source: In the transmitted resistance model, a patient accumulates a pool of mycobacteria with different genotypes during latent infection.

claim: The transmissibility of resistant variants has been confirmed through strain-specific PCR.
source: The transmissibility of resistant variants has been confirmed through strain-specific PCR (Braden et al., 2001)

source: and selective adaptation in a patient during chemotherapy has also been demonstrated (Hingley-Wilson et al., 2013).

claim: Clonal complexity is reduced by culturing, leading to the underrecognition of polyclonal infections in culture-based diagnosis.

claim: The WHO estimates that a quarter of the world's population is latently infected by M. tuberculosis.
source: The WHO estimates that a quarter of the world's population is latently infected by M. tuberculosis, accumulating different TB strains throughout their lives (World Health Organization, 2021).
